zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after the independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). The scan, not the lexical index or generated kana hints, determines the transcription.

lines.note: Sugui is described as a tree resembling a cypress; sugui ita means boards of its wood. The scan supports aruore and a full stop after ita, not OCR arure or a line-end hyphen.
Translates sugui ita as boards of this wood. It is a complete gloss on a separate physical row, not the continuation of a divided Japanese word.
The verb Sugui concerns time or something else passing. Its printed principal parts are preserved rather than expanded into modern verb forms.
Completes the general passing sense, then gives michi wo yuki suguru, going beyond one's destination or route. Paſ- begins the Portuguese verb below.

runs.text: ſar auante do lugar pera onde hum hia. ¶

lines.note: Completes the example as passing beyond the place one was heading for. The visible final vowel supports hia, not OCR hio; Mi begins the next Japanese expression without a printed hyphen.
Mi wo suguru and inochi wo suguru introduce the sense of getting through or sustaining one's life. Uo continues the particle after Mi across the physical break.

runs.text: vida, ou ſustentarſe. Item, Acabarſe. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the livelihood sense, then adds finishing or coming to an end. The following example illustrates the latter meaning.
Mexi suguita is glossed as having finished eating. The worn t in suguita and the abbreviated Itẽ are retained as the preferred scan readings.
Another sense is exceeding, with the complement treated as dative. Bunni suguita describes something beyond one's means; the scan supports t rather than OCR r in the verb.
Kirumono supplies the clothing in the example: this garment exceeds the speaker's means. Mi- begins Portuguese minha, not a Japanese element.
Completes minha poße, the speaker's means or resources. The historical Portuguese possessive phrase is not modernized.
Suguifara, also suibara, is a kind of writing paper. The scan supports papel ẽ rather than OCR parelẽ; the damaged i in Suguifara is corroborated by the reciprocal entry later on this page.

runs.text: que ſe eſcreuem as cartas de Iapão.

lines.note: Completes the paper's use: Japanese letters are written on it. The national name Iapão retains consonantal I and its printed tilde.
Suguimura is a place with many sugi trees. Suguis is a Japanese tree name pluralized inside the Portuguese explanation, and the scan corrects OCR Saguis.
Completes the comparison with cypresses. The source offers a resemblance, not a modern botanical classification.
Suguina is identified simply as a particular plant. The note does not replace this deliberately general gloss with a modern species name.
Suguinixi is a historical form meaning past or gone by. Its repetition begins examples with words for a time or occasion.
Coro and toqi complete the examples of a past time or occasion. Ho- belongs to Portuguese hora, continued below.
Completes hora and closes the past-time example. The short row is retained as a physical continuation.
Suguisari is passing away or ceasing. The following example applies that motion figuratively to grief.
Kanashimi suguisaru means sadness passing away. The Portuguese irſe, to go away, corrects OCR trſe and connects with Acabarſe.
Supplies sadness as the subject of ending or going away. The printed short s in tristeza is preserved.

runs.text: Modo de grangear, ou paſſar a vi-

lines.note: Suguiuai is a way of earning a living or sustaining life. The historical Japanese form is not replaced by its modern equivalent.
Completes vida, then gives suguiwai wo suru, making a living. The corresponding Portuguese explanation continues below.
Completes the alternative wording, sustaining oneself. This closes the livelihood entry.

runs.text: Caualo em que ſe não pode caual-

lines.note: Suguivma describes a horse that cannot be ridden. The internal v begins the uma element and is preserved in the diplomatic spelling.
Completes caualgar and gives the reason: the horse is too wild or fierce. Brauo is retained with its historical u/v value.

runs.text: Portas que nãotem pollo meyo tra-

lines.note: Suguixooji denotes doors lacking crosspieces in the middle. The printed caron and joined nãotem are retained.
Completes traueßas and limits the framing to the perimeter. The physical division and historical spelling remain unchanged.
Suguiyama is a mountain with many sugi trees. Suguis occurs within Portuguese and is marked for optional whole-word typeface review.
Suguiyuqi describes continuing to pass, as time does. The printed yuita is preserved as a historical principal part.
Completes tempo and the example of time passing. The abbreviated nasal spelling tẽ-/po is not expanded or rejoined.
Sugoi here means something fearful or solitary. The source's historical sense is not replaced by the familiar modern praise-word meaning.
Sugoſugoto is labelled an adverb describing a solitary manner or state. The repeated-looking Japanese sequence is retained as printed.
Completes solitario and adds alone as an equivalent. The grave accent on ſò remains source evidence.
Sugoxi means exceeding or overdoing and is said to attach to verb stems. The historical oita principal part is not normalized to a modern past form.
Completes raiz and illustrates the suffix-like use with nomisugosu, drinking too much. The damaged letters remain legible in context and are not replaced by a modern spelling.

runs.text: Beber demaſiadamente. ¶ Itẽ, Paßar a vida

lines.note: The first gloss is drinking excessively. The next sense concerns passing one's life or years; demaſiadamente is one printed word, not OCR demaſio damente.
Toshi wo sugosu exemplifies passing the years. The Portuguese verb begins at the end of this row and continues below.
Completes the years example, then introduces inochi wo sugosu, passing one's life. The separate physical hyphen is preserved again.
Completes the life-passing gloss and closes Sugoxi. This short continuation is not attached to the following adjective.
Suguna describes something straight or upright. The Japanese adjective and concise Portuguese gloss are retained without expanding their range of meanings.
Suguni is identified as the corresponding adverb, straight or directly. Its printed left alignment is retained even though it is morphologically related to Suguna.
Sugure means being excellent or surpassing others. The following horse example illustrates comparison rather than movement past a location.

runs.text: Coreua yono vma yorimo ſugureta, l,

lines.note: The example says this surpasses other horses. The scan contains both an opening paragraph mark and final l, omitted from the OCR; they introduce an alternative continuation below.
The alternative describes an exceptionally outstanding horse. The scan supports yoni, not yomi, and the worn Portuguese caualo is read as a single word.
Completes the superlative gloss, the best of all. The printed milhor is preserved rather than modernized to melhor.
Sugurete is the adverbial or connective form, glossed as excellently or more advantageously. The long Portuguese adverb is divided across the physical rows.
Completes auantajadamente and the adverbial gloss. It is not a separate entry or a repeated catchword.
Suguri means choosing or taking the best. The scan resolves the garbled Portuguese as Eſcolher, outomar o milhor; the close-set outomar and historical milhor are retained.
Suguri idaxi is selecting out, referred to the preceding choosing sense. The printed spacing and abbreviated aita form are not regularized.
Suguritate means selecting and assembling people or things. Ajun- starts the Portuguese verb that continues below.

runs.text: tar, ou por a parte como gente de guerra, &c.

lines.note: Completes ajuntar and adds setting aside, with fighting men as the example. The source gives a military application rather than restricting the verb exclusively to soldiers.
Sugurocu is compared with the board game called tabolas. The historical sugu- spelling is preserved, and Su- begins the repeated game name below.
Sugurocu wo utsu means playing the game. The Portuguese retains the printed à tabolas rather than supplying an expected plural article.

runs.text: Taboleiro em que ſe joga às

lines.note: Sugurocuban is the board on which that game is played. The Portuguese noun Taboleiro retains its historical spelling.
Completes the description of the game board. The line belongs to Sugurocuban, not to the player entry below.
Sugurocu vchi denotes a player of the game. The separate second-pass enlargement supports the open u in Iugador, not a normalized Iogador; the following row supplies an additional evaluative use.
The expression can sometimes mean a good player. The historical jugador is retained with u, consistent with Iugador on the preceding line.

runs.text: Taful, ou amigo de jugar às

lines.note: Sugurocuzuqi denotes someone fond of the game or a gambler. The worn headword is read continuously, and Portuguese Taful has f rather than OCR long s.
Completes the description of someone fond of playing tabolas. This closes the group of game-related entries.
Sugi here is a vein or sinew, not the tree Sugui in the other column. The distinct printed spelling is essential to the Japanese reading.

runs.text: Couſa enuiaſada que não vai direita

lines.note: Sugicai describes something oblique rather than straight. The scan supports the headword and Portuguese enuiaſada, correcting malformed OCR Sugic.i and enuraſada.

runs.text: de lado a lado, nem de canto a canto. ¶

lines.note: The gloss says it does not run straight from side to side or corner to corner. Su- begins the Japanese example and is roman, correcting the OCR's misplaced italic boundary.
Sugicai ni michi wo yuku means proceeding along an oblique or indirect route. En- begins the Portuguese adjective, whose unusual continuation is retained below.

Completes the printed en-/uiaſdo, apparently a defective form of the oblique-path adjective. The visible letter order is retained rather than silently repairing it to a modern or expected historical spelling.
Sugigane denotes iron rods or bars. The damaged u in the headword is read from its remaining strokes and the Japanese compound rather than OCR Sagigane.

runs.text: Linha, ou fio direito. ¶ Item, Li-

lines.note: Sugime is a straight line or thread, with an additional sense beginning as Li-/nha. The next rows apply the idea of a line to descent.
Completes line of descent, then describes a person of good lineage. The worn medial m is read as in the headword Sugime; Ho- is wholly Portuguese italic rather than a roman fragment.

runs.text: mem de boa geração, ou nobre.

lines.note: Completes Homem and glosses the person as of good lineage or noble. The printed social classification is reported without expanding it beyond the source.
Sugiri describes twisting or winding, compared with ivy climbing a tree. The historical Portuguese era is retained without inserting an h.

runs.text: trepando polla aruore: comummente ſe vſa ſoo

lines.note: The ivy winds as it climbs the tree. The usage note says the form is commonly used only in a particular tense; vſa and ſoo correct the OCR's damaged readings.
Completes the usage restriction, in the preterite. This is the dictionary's statement about the verb's common use, not an instruction to alter the listed forms.
Sugiri mogiru is referred to the same twisting sense. The abbreviated Idẽ remains unexpanded.

The verb Sui is glossed as kissing and also sucking or sipping. Enlarged reinspection supports a damaged ǔta, including its caron, rather than ita. Beijar is the chosen reading of the first gloss: the initial capital has damaged right-hand curves and remains a nonblocking B/P/E-shaped-glyph caveat; it is not visually as secure as the other letters.
Shiru wo suu means sipping or sucking up broth. The scan has an opening paragraph mark and a caron on the verb's u, both absent from the provisional transcription.
This Sui denotes conjecture or suspicion, paraphrased by the Japanese verb Voxi, ſu. It is distinct from sucking and from the sour adjective below.
Sui suru means to conjecture or suspect. The attached suru follows the print's spacing rather than a modern editorial separation.
The next homograph is the adjective sour. The Portuguese azeda directly distinguishes it from the preceding noun and verb.
These are the related form Suu and the noun for sourness, Susa. The caron is preserved as a printed vowel-length mark.
Suiague means raising something by sucking it up. The Portuguese ſoruendo corrects OCR ſorurndo and continues with aleuantar below.
Completes the sucking-up sense and begins an example in which clouds draw up water. The scan supports ſuiague-, not the malformed ſutague-.
Completes suiagete ame to nasu, drawing water up and making it rain. The Portuguese restates the example with clouds as the subject.
Completes the example: the clouds turn the water into rain. This reports the source's explanation and preserves the separated pronoun na.
Suibara is the paper name for which Suguifara is preferred. The scan supports b in Suibara and Papel aßi; this reciprocal entry corroborates the earlier paper entry.

runs.text: mado em que ſe eſcreuem as cartas de Iapão.

lines.note: Completes chamado and specifies paper used for Japanese letters. The capital in Iapão is interpreted as the same consonantal I used elsewhere on this page, rather than OCR L.
Suibi is gradual decline or deterioration, introduced through a Japanese explanatory phrase. The Portuguese begins becoming worse, with an alternative continuation below.
Completes the idea of being ruined little by little. The example begins a house's decline; the worn suibi has an i omitted by OCR, while its close attachment to Iyega is retained.
Suru completes the example of a house gradually falling apart or being ruined. The joined deſtruindoa remains as printed.
Suibin is a water vessel or ewer. Gumil is retained as the source's Portuguese vessel name rather than normalized to another form.

Suiboo is drinking to excess, paraphrased by yoi aku. The initial S corrects OCR D. The final marked form tẽ is retained from the aligned transcription: the ink above e is blotted and its exact shape remains uncertain; the continuation gives the sense 'until unable to drink more.'

Completes drinking until one can take no more, then begins an example about intoxication affecting the heart or mind. The conditional ſureba corrects OCR ſuroba; the example's unmarked Suibo is retained.
Kiooran su completes the mental-disturbance example. The Portuguese says that while drunk one becomes disturbed, with the manner specified below.

runs.text: interiormente, ou ſair fora de ſi.

lines.note: Completes the gloss as becoming inwardly disturbed or beside oneself. The scan resolves the garbled OCR and ends with a full stop, not a hyphen; the catchword below is separate furniture.
